analysis.one_liner: Lets taxpayers and businesses choose an optional flat tax instead of the regular income tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let any individual or business make an irrevocable choice to pay a flat tax instead of the regular income tax: 19% for the first two years, then 17%. Under the flat tax, a person's taxable income would be cash wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment benefits minus a large standard deduction; investment income such as capital gains, dividends, and interest would not be taxed at all. Businesses would pay 17% on their business income and government and nonprofit employers would pay a tax on fringe benefits they provide.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households come out best: the bill taxes only wages, retirement payouts, and unemployment benefits, so capital gains, dividends, and interest owed by wealthy taxpayers would escape tax entirely at a 17% rate on whatever wages they have. Businesses also gain from a low rate on a cash-flow base. Some working families gain on paper too: with a standard deduction of $25,580 for a couple plus $5,510 per child, a family of four earning roughly $47,000 or less in wages would owe no flat tax, and everyone who elects gets a much simpler return.

how_it_helps.text: Any individual or business could elect a flat tax of 19% for the first two years and 17% thereafter, in place of regular income tax rates that rise with income.
The flat tax base excludes capital gains, dividends, and interest entirely; individuals are taxed only on cash wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation.
A large standard deduction ($25,580 for joint filers plus $5,510 per dependent, indexed to inflation) would zero out tax for many lower-wage families who elect the system.
Businesses would pay 17% on business taxable income (gross receipts minus costs and wages), a much lower rate than the 35% corporate rate then in law.

analysis.who_pays: Because the election is voluntary, taxpayers would choose it whenever it lowers their bill, so the federal government would lose revenue, and that shortfall would have to be made up by borrowing, spending cuts, or higher taxes on people who stay in the regular system. Government agencies and tax-exempt employers would also pay a new 17% tax on fringe benefits like health coverage they provide to employees.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises no transition revenue and would likely cut federal receipts substantially, since taxpayers elect only when it lowers their taxes and capital income drops out of tax entirely.
Taxing only wages and not investment income shifts the overall tax burden toward working people, because wealth held in appreciated assets, dividends, and interest pays nothing.

The election is irrevocable, so a taxpayer who switches and later finds the flat tax costs more (for example after a large standard deduction or family change) cannot go back, with only a narrow exception for innocent-spouse relief.
Government agencies, state and local governments, and tax-exempt organizations would owe a new tax on the value of noncash employee benefits, raising their costs or forcing benefit cuts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers genuine simplification and a tax-free threshold for low-wage families, but its central trade is lopsided: it removes the top rates that fall on the highest earners and eliminates tax on investment income altogether. Because the election is one-way and voluntary, the government would lose the most revenue exactly from the taxpayers best positioned to switch, leaving either debt or higher burdens on those who remain. For a typical middle-income wage earner the gain is modest; for high earners with capital income it is large.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2003, sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess introduced the bill on April 11, 2003, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Twenty-three representatives cosponsored the bill, 21 Republicans and 2 Democrats.
The Ways and Means Committee took no further action; the only recorded activity after referral was Burgess's own remarks about the bill in April 2003 and April 2004.
The bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing tax code's structure stayed in place, which preserves the current tax treatment of investment income and the market for tax preparation and planning; no one gained the 17% business rate or the untaxed capital income the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supporters of the existing tax system

for.name: Rep. Michael Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and promoted it in floor remarks in April 2003 and again in April 2004.

for.name: 21 of 23 cosponsors (21 House Republicans and 2 House Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors such as Reps. Boehner, Burton, and Sessions.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, keeping it from reaching the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Republican project: 21 of its 23 cosponsors were Republicans, and it died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority without receiving action.

industries.note: The bill would exempt capital gains, dividends, and interest from tax entirely and cap the rate at 17%, letting wealthy households stop paying tax on their main income sources. The lost revenue would fall on everyone else through debt or future taxes.

Electing businesses would pay 17% instead of the up-to-35% corporate rate on a broad cash-flow base, cutting their tax bill. Lower business taxes can reach the public through prices and wages, but the direct beneficiary is owners.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: A flat tax with one rate and a standard deduction would sharply reduce demand for preparers and software, since returns become simple enough to file alone.

industries.industry: Government agencies and tax-exempt organizations as employers
industries.note: The bill imposes a 17% employer tax on the value of fringe benefits like health coverage at government and nonprofit employers, raising the cost of employing people there or cutting those benefits.
